$comment: Every number here traces to a measurement or to a stated assumption. A
round figure that felt right is not a budget — it is an obstacle with no
argument behind it, and the first person it inconveniences will delete it.
Two kinds of number live in this file and they must not be confused:
BASELINE — evidence. What the site measured on a stated date, machine
and commit. Re-recorded with `--record`; never edited by hand.
CEILING  — a decision. What the site is allowed to become. Changed only
deliberately, with the reason recorded in TASKS.md Decisions.
The gate enforces ceilings. A baseline is what a ceiling is derived from.

method.server: scripts/serve-static.mjs — Apache-parity static server over dist/public
why: Production is Apache on HostGator serving dist/public as static files:
else, so the Express app in dist/index.js is never deployed. Measuring
Lighthouse against Express measured the wrong server, and served every
Paired runs, identical build and profile, 2026-09-06, 3 runs each:
Express (uncompressed)  transfer 1,929,039 B  FCP 8,352 ms  LCP 11,844 ms
Apache-parity (gzip)    transfer 1,125,838 B  FCP 3,844 ms  LCP  7,824 ms
Compression is calibrated to the real host, not to `gzip -6`. Apache on
bytes as `gzip -6` for byte-identical input, measured by fetching each
live URL twice with Accept-Encoding: identity and gzip. See the header
of scripts/serve-static.mjs for the table and the parameter sweep that
cannotTellUs: Field performance. There is no RUM and no CrUX access from here, so no
claim about real visitors' 75th percentile is made anywhere in this file.
Every timing number is a Lighthouse Lantern SIMULATION on the profile
below, and Lantern models a device this machine is not.
Production is HTTP/2 over TLS; the parity server is HTTP/1.1 on localhost.
Google Fonts is fetched from its real origin, so a run needs internet.

profile.name: mobileSlow4G
derivation: These are Lighthouse's own default constants, read from
Chosen for three reasons, in order:
1. It is the default, so it is what any third party auditing this site
— a customer, a prospect, PageSpeed Insights — actually sees.
2. Google's Core Web Vitals 'good' thresholds, which the TARGETS below
are derived from, are defined against this class of device.
3. There is no analytics access from this repo, so the device mix is
UNKNOWN. Faced with an unmeasured assumption, the budget takes the
conservative side rather than the flattering one.
The previous script set formFactor 'desktop' and a desktop screen but
left throttling and the user agent at these mobile defaults: a desktop
viewport with a Moto G Power user agent on a slow-4G link at 4x CPU.
That is not a device, and no budget can be derived from it.
profile.downlinkDerivation: 1474.56 kbps downlink = 1,474,560 bits/s / 8 = 184,320 bytes/s. Every byte allowance below is stated in this unit.

document.derivation: Baseline + the 9,216 B standard allowance. index.html is served Cache-Control: max-age=0 (.htaccess:69), so unlike the hashed assets this is paid in full on EVERY page view, by every visitor, forever. It is 137,210 B because vite-plugin-manus-runtime injects 366,824 characters of inline parser-blocking JavaScript into it (see findings).

entryJs.derivation: Baseline + the 9,216 B standard allowance. Replaces the previous 270 kB gzip cap, which was a round figure with no derivation: 270,000 B of `gzip -6` is 7,399 B of headroom over a 262,601 B build, but it is measured in a unit production does not use — Apache puts 364,514 B of this chunk on the wire, 38.8% more than the number the cap governs.

entryCss.derivation: Baseline + the 9,216 B standard allowance. Render-blocking: the SPA cannot paint before it arrives.

criticalPath.derivation: document + entryJs + entryCss — everything a visitor must download before the page can paint anything. Baseline + ONE 9,216 B allowance, deliberately not the sum of the three individual allowances (which would be 27,648 B): the aggregate is what the visitor pays, so the aggregate gets one allowance. Spending the whole allowance on one asset therefore costs it from the others.

standardAllowanceDerivation: 9,216 B = 50 ms of download at the profile's 184,320 B/s.
Two independent lines pick 50 ms, which is why it is the number:
1. Google's RAIL guidance treats 100 ms as the threshold at which a
response stops feeling instantaneous. Half of that is a conservative
'not perceptible' increment for a single change.
2. The largest feature this repository has shipped — the entire 3D-7D
dimensional stack — added 5.52 kB gzip-6 to the entry chunk
(257.08 -> 262.60 kB, recorded in TASKS.md). At this build's measured
JS inflation factor of 1.388 that is 7,662 B of production transfer.
So the allowance admits one more feature the size of the biggest one
ever shipped, plus 20% margin, and nothing larger without a decision.
The allowance needs no noise margin: `npm run build` was run twice on
identical source and every output file matched by md5. Byte budgets are
deterministic, so they are enforced with zero tolerance.

fcp.derivation: 1.5x the worst value seen across the 5 baseline runs. FCP here is bimodal rather than noisy-around-a-centre: on byte-identical input it lands either at ~3,840 ms or at ~4,600-4,750 ms, a 17.1-23.6% spread, and the ~800 ms step is the render-blocking third-party stylesheet from fonts.googleapis.com on the critical path (client/index.html:21) resolving fast or slow. The ceiling is loose as a direct consequence of that finding, and it tightens when the font stylesheet leaves the critical path, not before.

lcp.derivation: 1.5x the worst of 5 baseline runs. LCP is the stable metric here - measured spread 0.2% (Home), 0.2% (Products), 6.3% (About) on byte-identical input, because Lantern derives it mostly from transfer size - so this is the ceiling most likely to catch a real regression.

si.derivation: 1.5x the worst of 5 baseline runs. Speed Index tracked FCP to the millisecond in every run measured, so it inherits FCP's bimodality and its derivation.

cls.derivation: Google's Core Web Vitals 'good' threshold, used verbatim. The one metric where the site is already comfortably inside the external standard - measured 0 to 0.0163, at least 6x better than the threshold - so an absolute external number is both honest and non-vacuous: any layout-shift regression that matters trips it.

performanceScore: The composite Lighthouse performance score is REPORTED and NOT GATED.
It is 30% TBT by weight, and TBT measured a 3.07x run-to-run spread on
byte-identical input — the same build scored 49, 60 and 62 in three
consecutive runs. A threshold on a number that moves 13 points without
the code changing is either flaky or vacuous; there is no third option.
The metrics the score is made of are gated individually above, which is
the same information without the noise.
accessibility/best-practices/seo: Measured and reported, not gated here. They are not performance, and
gating them from the performance script would put the accessibility
verdict somewhere no one reviewing accessibility would look.
tbt: Total Blocking Time is MEASURED AND REPORTED, NOT GATED.
On byte-identical input it measured 32.1% (About), 72.4% (Home) and
111.7% (Products) spread across 5 runs - Products produced 510 ms and
1,141 ms in the same set - and across every run taken this session Home
ranged 234-731 ms. A 1.5x-of-observed-max ceiling for Home would sit at
765 ms, which is inside the range already observed with nothing changed:
it would fail on noise. A ceiling wide enough not to fail on noise is
wide enough to miss any regression worth catching.
This is a property of the measurement, not of the site. It becomes
gateable on a machine with a quiet CPU, or with throttlingMethod
'provided' against real hardware. Until then a TBT threshold here would be
either flaky or decorative, and saying so is more useful than either.

timingRuleDerivation: Every gated timing ceiling is `1.5 x the worst value observed across the
baseline runs`, and every baseline is recorded with 5 runs per page.
WHY MAX-OF-N AND NOT A PERCENTAGE OF THE MEDIAN. Measured run-to-run
spread on BYTE-IDENTICAL input, 5 runs per page, 2026-09-06:
LCP  0.2% - 6.3%     stable; derived mostly from transfer size
FCP  17.1% - 23.6%   bimodal on the third-party font stylesheet
SI   17.1% - 23.6%   tracks FCP exactly
TBT  32.1% - 111.7%  tracks whatever else the machine is doing
A percentage-of-median tolerance tight enough to be useful for LCP would
false-FAIL on FCP about one run in five. Anchoring each ceiling to that
metric's own observed worst case gives every metric a headroom
proportional to its own measured noise, from a single rule, with no
per-metric hand-tuning.
WHY THE FACTOR IS 1.5 AND NOT SOMETHING SMALLER. It is set from a real
regression, then verified by causing that regression. The largest realistic
non-code regression this site can suffer is losing mod_deflate — one edit to
.htaccess and every asset ships uncompressed. That was forced directly, by
emptying DEFLATE_TYPES in scripts/serve-static.mjs and re-running this gate
(2026-09-06). Measured, against ceilings of FCP 6,918 / LCP 11,763 on Home:
Home      FCP 8,340   LCP 13,521   (baseline 3,854 / 7,832)
Products  FCP 8,350   LCP 13,006   (baseline 3,849 / 7,302)
About     FCP 8,348   LCP 13,003   (baseline 4,462 / 7,304)
Nine FAILs, exit 1. So 1.5x absorbs the measured noise AND still catches the
worst realistic regression. A larger factor would not; a smaller one would
false-FAIL on FCP's bimodality. The harness was restored immediately after.
The gate runs 1 run per page (PERF_RUNS, default 1) and finishes in about
55 s, inside the 300 s cap the verification gate applies to this check.

$comment: Where this site should be, as opposed to where it is. These are NOT
gated — the gate's job is to stop the site getting worse, and a gate
that fails on the day it is written stops being read. They are recorded
so the gap is a stated number rather than a vague sense that the site
feels slow, and so any future optimisation has something to aim at.
criticalPathDerivation: Derived from Google's 2.5 s 'good' LCP threshold on the profile above:
- 600 ms  connection setup (DNS + TCP + TLS + the extra RTT to discover
the CSS and JS referenced by the HTML, at 150 ms modelled RTT)
-  400 ms parse, compile, execute and first paint at 4x CPU slowdown
= 1500 ms left for transfer x 184,320 B/s = 276,480 B
Measured critical path is 533,605 B, which is 1.93x this target and
2,895 ms of download on its own — before a single byte is executed. So
the 2.5 s LCP objective is not reachable by tuning; 257,125 B has to
leave the critical path. Measured LCP is 7,824 ms.
STATUS: FAIL. Recorded as a gap, deliberately not gated.
targets.thresholdSource: Google Core Web Vitals 'good' thresholds (LCP 2.5 s, FCP 1.8 s, CLS 0.1).

baseline.$comment: Evidence, not decision. Rewritten by `PERF_RUNS=5 node tests/performance/lighthouse.mjs --record`. Do not hand-edit.
baseline.benchmarkIndexDerivation: Lighthouse's own CPU calibration score, read from lhr.environment.benchmarkIndex. The band is 0.7x to 1.6x of the recorded value. Within-session spread measured 1309.5-1440.5 (6 runs, +/-5%), so 0.7x cannot be reached by same-machine variation — it only trips on genuinely different hardware. Outside the band the timing budgets are reported UNKNOWN rather than FAIL or PASS, because a baseline recorded on one machine is not evidence about another. Byte budgets and route isolation gate regardless, since they are hardware-independent.
